newsitem.title: USA: Soy and corn acreage shift to dominate CBOT prices.
newsitem.headline: Soy and corn acreage shift to dominate CBOT prices.

text.p: The shift by U.S. farmers away from corn into soybean seedings this year will dominate CBOT futures price direction and the acreage change magnifies the impact of the Freedom to Farm Bill, analysts said.

"If anything can be gleaned it's that Freedom to Farm does work," said Dick Loewy, President of Chicago-based firm AgResource Inc. "We were mesmerized this spring by early plantings but we should have seen this coming."

USDA on Monday shocked the market by revealing a 1997 U.S. soybean acreage tally at 70.9 million acres, well above an average of analysts' expectations for 68.4 million. But corn acreage this year was pegged by USDA at 80.2 million, below expectations for 81.8 million bushels.

U.S. farmers, in a break from traditional government price supports and subsidies, are now operating with the most flexibile farm bill in recent memory. Freedom to Farm allows farmers nearly total freedom to make crop planting decisions.
Traders and analysts were expecting CBOT December corn futures to open two to three cents per bushel higher, but new-crop November beans were called to open five to 10 cents lower.

"The surprise to the report was the big change in acres," said Don Roose, CEO of U.S. Commodities Inc of Des Moines, Iowa. "With the new Freedom to Farm, the farmer is planting for profit so we have to look for big swings in acreages."
Roose, predicted the U.S. soy crop this year would average 39.5 bushels per acrea and corn 131 bushels an acre, based on current conditions. "But that could improve," he said.
Loewy pegged the 1997 U.S. soybean crop at 2.8 billion bushels based on 40.1 bushels per harvested acre and corn production this year at 10.1 billion bushels based on 138 bushels per harvested acre.

Roose and Loewy, along with Rand Financial Services Inc analyst Gregg Hunt, appeared at a CBOT sponsored press conference following the release at 0730 CDT Monday of USDA's acreage and quarterly stocks reports.
The analysts said the stocks data were about as expected with some support to nearby July soybeans coming from another reminder of tight soybeans stocks.
"The bean stocks number has to be construed as bullish and the corn stocks were pretty much in line with expectations," Loewy said.

USDA said the U.S. soybean supply as of June 1 totaled 499 million bushels, below expectations for 516 million. Corn stocks were at 2.49 billion bushels, above expectations for 2.478 billion and wheat stocks at 444 million bushels were below expectations for 466 million bushels.
Traders and analyst gave a bearish spin to wheat prices due to the USDA forecast that 19.2 million acres of spring wheat were planted this year, above expectations for 18.1 million.
"Another surprise was the spring wheat acres," Loewy said.
